rows.label: R. Eliezer (ר"א)
rows.why: Shmuel, an early Babylonian amora, explains the view of a tannaitic R. Eliezer on offspring and substitutes of an olah. The profile's links to Abaye and Shmuel in this passage fit R. Eliezer b. Hyrcanus.

rows.label: ר"א (abbreviated name, as written)
rows.why: A tanna would be cited with 'tanya' or a baraita rather than 'amar', though the abbreviation could also stand for Eliezer.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: A tannaitic Eliezer would be cited in a mishnah or baraita, not as 'והאמר ר"א' with a rabbinic-level ruling.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: ר"א could expand to Eliezer, and the passage does not exclude him.

rows.label: ר"א (the one who disqualifies in the mishna)
rows.why: Printed texts often read 'ר"א' as Rabbi Eliezer, a plausible alternative, but no passage evidence settles it.

rows.label: ר"א (R. Eliezer or R. Elazar; abbreviation left as written)
rows.why: Possible if the abbreviation means Eliezer, but the passage gives no cue; he is a less likely Mishnah eruv ruling here.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: A tanna; Zerika, an amora, would not cite him as 'ר"א' in this way.

rows.label: ר"א בן דורדיא
rows.why: The name Eliezer is abbreviated ר"א, but Eliezer b. Hyrcanus has a different patronym and is not the man in this story.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: The sugya treats this as an amoraic ruling that is being tested, not a tannaitic dispute. Nothing points to him.

rows.label: Rabbi Elazar (ר"א)
rows.why: The abbreviation ר"א could stand for Eliezer, but the full name 'R. Elazar' in the following sources points elsewhere, and he is an earlier tanna.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: The abbreviation ר"א could stand for Eliezer, but the passage's amoraic exchange with R. Yochanan points elsewhere.

rows.label: רבי אלעזר / ר"א (s4)
rows.why: Is a generation earlier; 'ר"א' here as 'R. Elazar' fits the Meir circle better.

rows.label: ר"א (abbreviated sage, as written)
rows.why: A tannaitic Eliezer would normally be written in full, and 'the law follows' rulings in this sugya concern amoraic opinions.

rows.label: ר"א בן עזריה
rows.why: His patronymic is ben Hyrcanus, not ben Azaryah; the text gives 'ben Azaryah'.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: The abbreviation could stand for Eliezer, but this ruling is attributed to the amora R. Elazar, and no tannaitic setting is indicated.

rows.label: ר"א (abbreviated name)
rows.why: Plausible as the Mishnah's Rabbi Eliezer, but the abbreviated name alone does not settle it.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: Would be abbreviated ר"א too, but the Gittin 'R. Elazar' dispute is less likely to be R. Eliezer.

rows.label: ר"א בן עזריה
rows.why: Father is Hyrcanus, not Azaryah.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: An abbreviated 'ר"א' could stand for Eliezer, but a tanna is usually written in full as 'ר' אליעזר' in such a chain.

rows.label: ר"א (abbreviated)
rows.why: A tanna; the dispute with the amora R. Shmuel b. Nachmani has no tannaitic setting.

rows.label: R. A. (as written 'ר"א')
rows.why: He was an early tanna and would normally be written 'R. Eliezer', not abbreviated 'ר"א' in an amoraic formula.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: The name is abbreviated 'ר"א', which could be Eliezer, but the Mishnah's context points to Elazar.

rows.label: ר"א (abbreviation)
rows.why: Would normally be written 'ר"א' only for a tanna; here the context is an amoraic dispute over Beit Shammai's ma'amar.

rows.label: ר"א (abbreviation, ambiguous)
rows.why: He is the tanna whose view is being explained, not the amora commenting on the dispute.

rows.label: ר"א (abbreviated name)
rows.why: A tanna would not be paired with Resh Lakish in an amoraic Gemara dispute over the source.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: The abbreviation could stand for Eliezer, but the Mishnah usually writes 'R. Eliezer' in full, and nothing here points to him.

rows.label: R. Elazar ben Azarya (ר"א בן עזריה)
rows.why: The text gives 'ben Azarya', not Eliezer b. Hyrcanus.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: He is a Shammaite-leaning tanna, but he is usually named R. Eliezer and is earlier than the R. Shimon and Abba Shaul named here.

rows.label: ר"א (abbreviation as written; holds that witnesses of delivery effect divorce)
rows.why: He was an earlier tanna, not R. Meir's usual counterpart in this dispute, and the abbreviation reads as Elazar.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: The abbreviation 'ר"א' here appears in an amoraic context after R. Yochanan, so a tanna is less likely.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: A tannaitic figure; the passage gives no sign of a baraita or Mishnah ruling.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: The abbreviation is usually R. Eliezer, written "ר"א", though that is possible.

rows.label: R. Elazar (written as ר"א and as רבי אלעזר)
rows.why: Spelled אלעזר in full; Eliezer b. Hyrcanus is not associated with the ribui-u-miut method, which is Akiva's.

rows.label: ר"א (abbreviation, kept as written)
rows.why: The abbreviation is more likely R. Elazar than R. Eliezer, and the Amoraic debate with R. Yitzchak and Rava points to a later period.

rows.label: ר"א (abbreviated name, not expanded)
rows.why: He could be abbreviated ר"א, but nothing in the passage points to a tannaitic dispute involving him.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: The abbreviation ר"א here is a Land of Israel amora in the R. Yochanan circle, not the early tanna R. Eliezer.

rows.label: ר"א (abbreviation, unexpanded)
rows.why: The abbreviation could stand for Eliezer, but the chronology and Shmuel's citation habits favor Elazar.

rows.label: ר"א, explaining speaker
rows.why: A tanna, so he would be the authority being explained, not the amoraic speaker.

rows.label: ר"א בן יעקב
rows.why: His name does not carry the patronymic 'ben Yaakov'.

rows.label: ר"א (abbreviated name, not expanded)
rows.why: He is a tanna, and the sequence of amoraic revisions (Rava, Rav Papa) suggests an amora. His name is normally written in full.

rows.label: R. A. (ר"א, as written)
rows.why: The abbreviation is for Elazar, and the passage is amoraic, so R. Eliezer is not indicated.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: Tanna of an earlier generation; would not be paired with R. Yochanan in an amoraic dispute.

rows.label: R. Eliezer (ר"א)
rows.why: He was R. Akiva's teacher, not a follower of his method, so 'in R. Akiva's method' does not fit.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: Paired with R. Yochanan as amoraic disputants, so a tanna is unlikely; the Eliezer reading is not supported.

rows.label: ר"א in s3 (Rabbi Eliezer or Rabbi Elazar)
rows.why: A tanna of an earlier period; Abbahu's 'amar R. Elazar' formula points to an amora.

rows.label: R. Eleazar
rows.why: His name is Eliezer, not Eleazar, and nothing in the passage points to him.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: Abbreviation ר"א could be Eliezer, but the Mishnah here more likely means Elazar.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: A tanna who is cited separately in the baraita; he could not be reporting Hoshaya, an amora.

rows.label: ר"א (abbreviation as written)
rows.why: 'ר"א' could abbreviate Eliezer, but the Mishnah usually writes Eliezer in full and he belongs to an earlier generation.

rows.label: ר"א (Rabbi E., abbreviated)
rows.why: A tanna; the abbreviation is more often used for the amora, and nothing in the passage ties it to him.

rows.label: ר"א / Rabbi Elazar
rows.why: He is the tanna whose position is being explained ("כחו דרבי אליעזר"), not the amoraic speaker.

rows.label: ר"א (the questioner, abbreviated name as written)
rows.why: A tanna; amoraic bavi'a-style questions about Rabba and Rav Yosef do not fit him.

rows.label: R. El'azar (abbr. ר"א)
rows.why: The abbreviation ר"א could stand for Eliezer, but the pairing with R. Yonatan points to an amoraic Elazar.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: Tannaitic, not a contemporary of R. Yochanan; the pairing with R. Yochanan points to an amora.

rows.label: R. A. (ר"א, R. Elazar or R. Eliezer as printed)
rows.why: A tanna would normally appear in a mishnah or baraita, not as a bare 'amar' statement discussed by amoraim.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: Considered the likely candidate, but a mishnaic debate about 'protection' may involve R. Elazar instead.

rows.label: ר"א
rows.why: Tannaitic Eliezer is normally named 'ר"א' only in tannaitic contexts; this is an amoraic-style ruling cited in a later discussion.
